syllabus.clause: subtree-size augmentation for rank and select in O(log n)

at.step: One extra number per node: the size of its own subtree, including itself. Each one is just its children's sizes, plus one for itself.
Want the fifth-smallest key? Compare it against the left subtree's size. Too big, subtract and go right. Too small, go left. Exactly right, stop.
Rank runs the same trick upward: climb to the root, and every time the path climbs up from a right child, add that side's whole left subtree to the count.

syllabus.clause: the general rule for which augmentations survive rotations

at.step: Size survives a rotation because it's computed from just a node and its two children. Any augmented field with that property survives the same way, at the same cost.

This topic deliberately augments topic 24's identical red-black tree rather than building a fresh balanced structure, because the point is that augmentation is cheap on top of an already-solved balancing problem.

at.step: A balanced tree answers whether a key is here in order log n. It says nothing about that key's rank among everything else in the tree. A small amount of bookkeeping, and that question is answered too.

items.item: The insert-path size update and the insert's own BST-property walk are the same walk — the augmentation costs nothing beyond what insert was already doing, not a separate O(log n) pass.

at.step: One new key, one path, one increment at every node along it — never a re-scan of anything beneath.

items.item: A valid size field and a valid BST/colour invariant are independent facts about a tree; this topic's predict step tests specifically whether a learner assumes the whole tree is disturbed by either an insert or a rotation, rather than only the directly affected nodes.

items.item: This topic's own measured numbers (comparison counts tied to height, exactly two sizes changed by one isolated rotation) are honest measurements on one real augmented tree, not claimed as a universal worst case beyond what the sources themselves state.
Interval trees apply the identical general rule to a different field (max endpoint rather than size); this topic names that connection without re-teaching interval trees, which the syllabus skips.

Ranks themselves aren't stored directly at each node because they would be expensive to maintain under tree modification, which is exactly why subtree sizes (a locally-computable field) are stored instead and rank is derived from them on demand.
